facts.claim: "Too Stoned to Cry (2019 Recut)" is a newly re-recorded version of a song from Andrew Combs' 2012 debut album Worried Man. It appears on the Worried Man (Deluxe Edition) reissue, alongside a recut of "Take It From Me".
Combs said he had always wanted to re-record the song. He said he loves it but can't stand his vocal take on the original, and that he sounded "so young and pitchy".
Combs described the recut as an updated version that somewhat replicates how his band plays it every night on the road.
The recut was released digitally ahead of the album as the first track from the deluxe reissue. The reissue was handled by New West Records, and by Loose Records in the UK/EU.
The Bandcamp credits for the deluxe edition say all songs were written by Andrew Combs, apart from "Heavy" and "Come Tomorrow". The album credits list production by Mike Odmark and Andrew Combs.

The credited band on the Worried Man album is Jon Radford (drums, percussion), Mike Rinne (bass), Micah Hulscher (piano, organ), Spencer Cullum Jr. (pedal steel, dobro, backing vocals), Jeremy Fetzer (lead guitar, backing vocals) and Combs (rhythm guitar, backing vocals). These are the credits for the original 2012 album. They are not specific to the 2019 recut.
The 2019 recut runs 3:24, against 3:37 for the original album version.
Rolling Stone Country said Worried Man (2012) showed flashes of brilliance on songs like "Too Stoned to Cry". It also noted appearances by Caitlin Rose and Spencer Cullum Jr.
A London live review noted that Combs re-cut the track from his 2012 self-funded Worried Man album, and that it is one of his favourite songs to sing live.

Combs was born in Dallas, Texas, on December 19, 1986, and moved to Nashville to pursue music. AllMusic describes him as pairing indie Americana with vintage country-pop in the vein of Mickey Newbury, Harry Nilsson and Townes Van Zandt.

research.lineage: Combs is a Dallas-born, Nashville-based singer-songwriter in the indie Americana and country-folk tradition, which AllMusic compares to Mickey Newbury, Harry Nilsson and Townes Van Zandt.

draft:
The cruelest joke in **Too Stoned to Cry** is that the drugs don't kill the pain. They only take away the release. Andrew Combs builds the whole song on that trap. The narrator is lonesome and bled dry, and the one thing that would let any of it out is the thing he's too far gone to do. Each time the refrain comes around, the last word changes. First it's *cry*, then *fly*, then *die*: "I keep tryin' / But I'm too stoned to die." That's the turn. It's not quite a death wish, and it's not quite a confession. It reads more like a man noticing that even giving up is out of reach.

Combs wrote it for his self-funded 2012 debut, *Worried Man*. Rolling Stone Country singled it out as one of that record's flashes of brilliance. He said he always loved the song but couldn't stand his original vocal, which sounded "so young and pitchy" to him. So he cut it again for the 2019 deluxe reissue, aiming for something close to how his band plays it every night on the road. It's one of his favorite songs to sing live, and the recut has that worn-in ease.

The arrangement stays gentle. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through arpeggiated chords over a simple bass line. The drums are light, with brushes on the snare, and a clean electric guitar sings a sustained melody against the vocal. The tempo is slow, with a relaxed sway, and the room sound is natural and unfussy. Combs sings in a slightly raspy, conversational voice, and he doesn't push. Nobody harmonizes with him. That fits a song this alone.

The lineage is plain. The opening pairing of "lonesome" with being too stoned to cry bends one of country's oldest lament phrases into something numbed out. AllMusic places Combs near Townes Van Zandt and Mickey Newbury. You can hear that kinship in the fatalism without melodrama. The catalog in the middle is whiskey, wine, pills, cocaine and easy women, all delivered as flatly as a grocery list. The sea imagery carries more of the feeling, in "I'm a sailor who's cold in the worst kind of storm." He even writes off salvation in a single shrug, saying the promise of Jesus was a lie.

What lingers is the gap between the words and the voice. The narrator insists he isn't happy, only numb, yet the band plays with real warmth. The song makes you feel grief that someone has sealed off from himself, and you end up doing the crying for him.
